--- title: "Interaction Terms" subtitle: "When the effect of one variable depends on another" author: "Prof. Eric Friedlander" footer: "[🔗 MATH 2025 - Fall 2026 - Schedule](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/)" logo: "../images/logo.png" format: revealjs: theme: slides.scss multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: false incremental: false chalkboard: true html-math-method: method: mathjax url: "https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/mathjax@3/es5/tex-mml-chtml.js" execute: freeze: auto echo: true cache: false knitr: opts_chunk: R.options: width: 200 bibliography: references.bib --- # Review: AE 17 ## Where we are {.smaller} Last time we fit our first multiple regression on the coffee truck: `Sales` from `Temperature` **and** a categorical variable. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:----------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 116.93| 20.75| 5.64| 0.00| |Temperature | -0.72| 0.35| -2.07| 0.04| |LocationCityHall | -3.88| 4.24| -0.91| 0.36| |LocationPark | 11.48| 4.13| 2.78| 0.01| |LocationZoo | -17.39| 4.21| -4.13| 0.00| ::: ::: ::: question Interpret the `Temperature` coefficient and the `LocationZoo` coefficient. What does the fitted picture look like? ::: . . . - `Temperature`: holding `Location` constant, each extra °F is associated with about 0.72 fewer cups. - `LocationZoo`: holding `Temperature` constant, the Zoo sells about 17 fewer cups than the Business District. - The fitted picture is **parallel lines**: one slope, one intercept per location. # Prediction ## Prediction {.smaller} ::: question How many bikes do we expect on a 25°C summer day? ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} new_day <- tibble(temp_orig = 25, season = "summer") predict(mlr_fit, new_day) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1 5041.681 ``` ::: ::: ## Cautions {.smaller} - **Do not extrapolate!** With several predictors you can extrapolate in many directions at once, even when each predictor is individually in range. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |season | min_temp| max_temp| |:------|--------:|--------:| |winter | 2.4| 23.5| |spring | 10.4| 33.1| |summer | 19.2| 35.3| |fall | 9.1| 27.0| ::: ::: ::: question Would you trust a prediction for a 30°C winter day? ::: . . . - The model shows **association, not causation**. Season and temperature are tangled together in observational data. ## Activity: Parts 4-5 {.smaller} ::: appex 📋 [AE 17 - Multiple Linear Regression with the Coffee Truck](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/ae/ae-17-mlr-coffee-truck.html) ::: - Part 4: predict `Sales` for a new day, and find a prediction you should not trust. - Part 5: reflection on $R^2$ and on randomized vs. observational data. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## From parallel lines to interactions {.smaller} Every model so far has been **additive**: the effect of one variable is the same at every value of the other. In a plot, that means **parallel lines**. ::: question Is it believable that an extra degree adds the same number of rentals in winter as in summer? That City Hall beats the Business District by the same amount at every time of day? ::: . . . Today: 1. A model with two predictors is a **surface**. An interaction **twists** it. 2. Three cases, one picture each: **two categorical** (group means), **one of each** (lines), **two quantitative** (a surface). 3. **AE 18**. # A model is a surface ## Two predictors, one surface {.smaller} With two explanatory variables $X_1$ and $X_2$, the mean of $Y$ is a **surface** above the $(X_1, X_2)$ plane. $$ \text{additive:}\quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 $$ . . . A **flat, tilted plane**. Fix $X_2$ and you get a line in $X_1$ with slope $\beta_1$. Change $X_2$ and the line just slides up or down: **parallel lines**. . . . $$ \text{with interaction:}\quad \mu_Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 X_1 + \beta_2 X_2 + \beta_3 X_1 X_2 $$ Fix $X_2$ and the slope in $X_1$ is $\beta_1 + \beta_3 X_2$: it **changes** with $X_2$. The plane gets a **twist**. # Case 1: Two categorical variables ## The data {.smaller} Same experiment as AE 17 and HW 08, but now we use **every** shift (Morning, Lunch, and Afternoon). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Rows: 180 Columns: 4 $ Location "Zoo", "Business", "Park", "Zoo", "Business", "Zoo", "City… $ TimeOfDay Morning, Lunch, Afternoon, Morning, Lunch, Afternoon, Morn… $ Temperature 63, 56, 66, 63, 62, 59, 56, 60, 59, 61, 60, 66, 54, 53, 63… $ Sales 18, 82, 74, 0, 58, 73, 44, 81, 78, 37, 87, 48, 66, 80, 77,… ``` ::: ::: - `Sales` (cups): our response. - `Location`: Business, CityHall, Park, or Zoo. - `TimeOfDay`: Morning, Lunch, or Afternoon. - `Temperature` (°F): recorded each shift. ## Modeling `Sales` from time and location {.smaller} Let's start with what we know: an **additive** model with both predictors (Business District vs. City Hall). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} add_fit <- lm(Sales ~ Location + TimeOfDay, data = bc) add_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 62.76| 3.23| 19.43| 0.00| |LocationCityHall | -5.84| 3.23| -1.81| 0.07| |TimeOfDayLunch | 20.57| 3.96| 5.20| 0.00| |TimeOfDayAfternoon | 14.23| 3.96| 3.60| 0.00| ::: ::: This model says the City Hall vs. Business difference is **the same** at every time of day. ## How good is this model? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: question Lines show the model's predicted mean for each group. How could the model be better? ::: ## What do the data say? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Location | Morning| Lunch| Afternoon| |:--------|-------:|-----:|---------:| |Business | 74.5| 71.3| 77.3| |CityHall | 45.1| 89.5| 70.9| ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=65%} ::: ::: ::: question Is City Hall better than the Business District? What would you tell Jo? ::: ## It depends! {.smaller} - **Morning:** City Hall sells about 29 *fewer* cups. - **Lunch:** City Hall sells about 18 *more* cups. - **Afternoon:** City Hall sells about 6 *fewer* cups. . . . When the effect of `Location` **depends on** `TimeOfDay`, we say there is an **interaction** between `Location` and `TimeOfDay`. . . . ::: question HW 08 only looked at Lunch. Why was that a good idea? What would we miss if we pooled all three shifts? ::: # The interaction model ## Adding an interaction {.smaller} To let the `Location` effect differ by `TimeOfDay`, we add the **product** of the indicator variables: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} int_fit <- lm(Sales ~ Location * TimeOfDay, data = bc) int_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------------------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 74.53| 3.04| 24.50| 0.00| |LocationCityHall | -29.40| 4.30| -6.83| 0.00| |TimeOfDayLunch | -3.27| 4.30| -0.76| 0.45| |TimeOfDayAfternoon | 2.73| 4.30| 0.64| 0.53| |LocationCityHall:TimeOfDayLunch | 47.67| 6.08| 7.84| 0.00| |LocationCityHall:TimeOfDayAfternoon | 23.00| 6.08| 3.78| 0.00| ::: ::: `Location * TimeOfDay` is shorthand for `Location + TimeOfDay + Location:TimeOfDay`. ## The model equation {.smaller} With the reference levels Business and Morning: $$ \begin{aligned} \widehat{\text{Sales}} = &\hat\beta_0 \\ &+ \hat\beta_1 \,\text{CityHall} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{Lunch} + \hat\beta_3 \,\text{Afternoon} \\ &\underbrace{+ \hat\beta_4 \,(\text{CityHall} \times \text{Lunch}) + \hat\beta_5 \,(\text{CityHall} \times \text{Afternoon})}_{\text{interaction terms}} \end{aligned} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: $$ \begin{aligned} \widehat{\text{Sales}} = &74.5 \\ &-29.4 \,\text{CityHall} -3.3 \,\text{Lunch} +2.7 \,\text{Afternoon} \\ &\underbrace{+47.7 \,(\text{CityHall} \times \text{Lunch}) +23.0 \,(\text{CityHall} \times \text{Afternoon})}_{\text{interaction terms}} \end{aligned} $$ ::: question For each of the six combinations of location and time of day, which terms are "on"? Write the equation for each one. ::: ## Recovering the cell means {.smaller} Each of the six means is the sum of the terms that are "on": ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Combination |Terms on | Model value| |:-------------------|:-----------------|-----------:| |Business, Morning |b0 | 74.5| |Business, Lunch |b0 + b2 | 71.3| |Business, Afternoon |b0 + b3 | 77.3| |CityHall, Morning |b0 + b1 | 45.1| |CityHall, Lunch |b0 + b1 + b2 + b4 | 89.5| |CityHall, Afternoon |b0 + b1 + b3 + b5 | 70.9| ::: ::: . . . The interaction model reproduces all six means exactly. It has one parameter per cell. ## Interpreting the interaction terms {.smaller} - $\hat\beta_1$ (`LocationCityHall`): City Hall minus Business **in the Morning** (the reference time). It is *not* the overall City Hall effect anymore. - $\hat\beta_4$ (`LocationCityHall:TimeOfDayLunch`): how much **bigger** the City Hall vs. Business difference is at Lunch than in the Morning. A difference in differences. - $\hat\beta_5$: the same, comparing Afternoon to Morning. . . . ::: question Use the coefficients to find the City Hall minus Business difference at Lunch. Does it match the table of means we saw earlier? ::: # Case 2: One of each ## Is the temperature slope the same in every season? {.smaller} Last time we fit `count ~ temp_orig + season`: one slope for temperature, a different intercept for each season. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question How well do these parallel lines follow the data in each season? ::: ## Letting the slope depend on season {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](18-interactions_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=80%} ::: ::: ::: question Which season has a very different slope? (Careful: each line only covers the temperatures that occur in its season.) ::: ## Slopes by season {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} season_int |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:----------------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | -111.0| 321.3| -0.3| 0.7| |temp_orig | 222.4| 24.9| 8.9| 0.0| |seasonspring | 1513.4| 571.8| 2.6| 0.0| |seasonsummer | 6233.0| 1079.3| 5.8| 0.0| |seasonfall | 2188.5| 535.0| 4.1| 0.0| |temp_orig:seasonspring | -61.6| 32.4| -1.9| 0.1| |temp_orig:seasonsummer | -238.9| 43.3| -5.5| 0.0| |temp_orig:seasonfall | -69.5| 34.5| -2.0| 0.0| ::: ::: - Winter (the reference level): slope $\hat\beta_1$ = 222 rentals per °C. - Summer: slope $\hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3$ = -16 rentals per °C. ::: question What would it mean for the summer slope to be about zero? ::: # Case 3: Two quantitative ## Temperature and time {.smaller} Bike share kept growing over the two years of data. Let's ask whether warm days mattered **more** later on. - $X_1$ = temperature (°C), $X_2$ = `instant`, the day number (1 to 731). $$ \widehat{\text{count}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \,\text{temp} + \hat\beta_2 \,\text{day} + \hat\beta_3 \,(\text{temp} \times \text{day}) $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} quant_add <- lm(count ~ temp_orig + instant, data = bikeshare) quant_int <- lm(count ~ temp_orig * instant, data = bikeshare) quant_xs <- seq(min(bikeshare$temp_orig), max(bikeshare$temp_orig), length.out = 30) quant_ys <- seq(min(bikeshare$instant), max(bikeshare$instant), length.out = 30) quant_labels <- c("Temperature (°C)", "Day number", "Daily rentals") ``` ::: ## Additive: a flat plane {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: The temperature slope is $\hat\beta_1 =$ 141 rentals per °C on **every** day. ## Interaction: a twisted surface {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
``` ::: ::: ::: question Compare the edge at day 1 with the edge at day 731. Where is the surface steeper in the temperature direction? ::: ## The slope is now a function {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} quant_int |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-----------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 645.590| 191.168| 3.377| 0.001| |temp_orig | 93.453| 9.745| 9.590| 0.000| |instant | 2.424| 0.486| 4.984| 0.000| |temp_orig:instant | 0.140| 0.024| 5.782| 0.000| ::: ::: $$ \text{slope of temp} = \hat\beta_1 + \hat\beta_3 \times \text{day} $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Day| Slope of temperature| |---:|--------------------:| | 1| 94| | 365| 145| | 731| 196| ::: ::: . . . For a fixed day, the slope of temperature is a number. As the day changes, the slope changes **linearly**: that is what a product term does. ## An interaction we don't need {.smaller} What about temperature and humidity? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |term | estimate| std.error| statistic| p.value| |:-------------|--------:|---------:|---------:|-------:| |(Intercept) | 2112.4| 695.5| 3.0| 0.0| |temp_orig | 197.2| 35.0| 5.6| 0.0| |hum | -1568.5| 1150.5| -1.4| 0.2| |temp_orig:hum | -48.8| 57.2| -0.9| 0.4| ::: ::: ::: question The interaction coefficient is small relative to its standard error, and $R^2$ barely moves. What would the surface look like? Would you add the term? ::: # The three cases ## Same idea, three pictures {.smaller} | | Two categorical | One of each | Two quantitative | |:---|:---|:---|:---| | Example | `Location` x `TimeOfDay` | `temp_orig` x `season` | `temp_orig` x `instant` | | Picture | jitter plot with group means | scatterplot with fitted lines | 3D surface | | Additive model | same gap between groups at every level (parallel profiles) | parallel lines | flat tilted plane | | Interaction adds | the 4th corner (a twist) | a different slope per group | a slope that changes with $X_2$ | | $\hat\beta_3$ means | difference in differences | the **change in slope** from the reference group | change in the slope of $X_1$ per unit of $X_2$ | . . . In all three cases, the interaction term is $X_1 \times X_2$, and it is what **bends** the surface. # Choosing a model ## Do we need the interaction? {.smaller} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} |model | r.squared| sigma| |:----------------------------|---------:|------:| |Coffee: Location + TimeOfDay | 0.269| 15.3| |Coffee: Location * TimeOfDay | 0.578| 11.8| |Bikes: temp + season | 0.456| 1433.1| |Bikes: temp * season | 0.478| 1406.4| |Bikes: temp + day | 0.686| 1087.2| |Bikes: temp * day | 0.700| 1063.8| |Bikes: temp + humidity | 0.427| 1468.7| |Bikes: temp * humidity | 0.427| 1469.0| ::: ::: ::: question Which interaction is worth adding? How do you know? (Think about $R^2$, $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$, and the pictures.) ::: . . . - A real interaction should show up in the plot, the $R^2$, and the size of the interaction coefficients relative to $\hat{\sigma}_\epsilon$. - Every interaction adds parameters. Add one when the picture and the context call for it. - We will learn formal tools for this later. ## Interactions and "holding constant" {.smaller} Last time: a coefficient is the change in the mean response per unit change in that predictor, **holding the other predictors constant**. . . . With an interaction, that sentence is incomplete: - There is **no single** effect of `Location`. There is one for each time of day. - Always describe the effect **at a particular value** of the other variable. . . . ::: question Jo asks, "How much better is City Hall?" What should you say back? ::: ## Activity: AE 18 {.smaller} ::: appex 📋 [AE 18 - Interactions with the Coffee Truck](https://ericfriedlander.github.io/math2025-fa26/ae/ae-18-interactions-coffee-truck.html) ::: - Each group gets a different pair of locations. - Build the table of means, plot the interaction, and fit both the additive and interaction models. - Recommend where Jo should park for each shift. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: ## Recap {.smaller} - An **interaction** means the effect of one variable depends on the value of another. - Categorical x categorical: the interaction terms are "differences in differences". - Categorical x quantitative: each group gets its own slope (parallel lines become non-parallel). - Quantitative x quantitative: the slope of one variable changes **linearly** with the other. - Geometrically, an additive model is a **flat plane** and an interaction **twists** it. - With an interaction, main effects are the effects at the reference level, not overall effects. - An additive model can hide a big pattern. Plot the data first. . . . **Next time:** we have a lot of estimates, like "City Hall sells 18 more cups at Lunch". How sure are we? **Confidence intervals.**

  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current

    // dispatch for htmlwidgets

      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);

    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {

          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
